rv.q: This is unrelenting – but magnificent.
It is brutally miserable, but somehow also mercifully entertaining.
It's been staged here with consummate skill and Norton's astonishing performance puts him into the top rank.
Norton's is, though, an astonishing performance in a production that leaves its mark like a livid, tender bruise on the imagination.
...here’s my content warning: the exposition-heavy script is as overstated as the accompanying string music – a little less of it, in fact a lot less of it, would help.
At its best it is transfixing. At its worst it is like a blind date between several episodes of Friends and the Oberammergau passion play.
But it filled me with utter gloom at the soul-crushing pointlessness of seeing these sufferings at such length.
Brilliant acting, great direction, but at heart it’s simply an empty vision of despair.
There’s something here that is deeply unsettling.
Although Norton convinces as Jude at every stage, his character is a cipher in itself – a patron saint of pain, an obscured Jude who is wholly defined by his abuse.
But the play itself is an unrelenting steeplechase of agonies, a punishment beating in its own right.
A stylishly mounted, second-rate melodrama.
A deeply moving and affecting piece of theatre, A Little Life is unflinching and searing in its portrayal of just how awful life can be.
It’s not an easy show to recommend, because it’s not an easy show to watch.
That is still a long haul, but von Hove’s production is constantly engaging, you don’t notice the time pass.
At the close, I felt I had witnessed a terrible, truthful depiction of the ongoing effects of mankind’s capacity for cruelty.
It's only a shadow of the book, but, realistically, this is probably the best adaptation fans and sceptics will get.

For all its theatrical power, however, I’m unconvinced A Little Life offers more than crude emotional manipulation, leaving me acutely upset rather than moved, and none the wiser about the human condition.
Despite a moment of undoubted shock and the winning of sympathy for Jude’s plight, ultimately the work on display feels more admirable than moving.
I think that A Little Life is a play that hates people, and especially damaged people.
The surfeit of gore is enervating and boring, not moving.
Whoever you are as you approach the Theatre, you'll leave someone else, having seen and heard things that can never be unseen or unheard.
Prepare for an ordeal rather than an entertainment.
You applaud his commitment while feeling disconnected from the material.

Director Ivo van Hove distils Hanya Yanagihara's novel into three and a half hours of utterly compelling theatre to examine a life lived under the scourge of guilt and a self-imposed exile from absolution.

cn.t: Van Hove's adaptation of Yanagihara's controversial novel proves divisive: critics praise Norton's towering, emotionally raw performance but split sharply on whether the nearly four-hour runtime and graphic depictions of trauma constitute art or endurance test.
